blogs.title: Acquired Ondine’s Curse: When Chiari I Triggers Central Hypoventilation
blogs.description: Explore how cerebellar tonsillar herniation can produce an acquired form of central hypoventilation that mimics congenital Ondine’s curse. The post will walk clinicians through the physiologic distinction between voluntary (cortical) and automatic (brainstem) breathing control, highlight key bedside clues such as severe desaturation without dyspnea during sleep or distraction, and outline a step‑by‑step diagnostic approach that incorporates history, arterial blood gases, overnight oximetry and neuroimaging. A brief review of the literature on brainstem compression‑related respiratory failure will reinforce why structural lesions must be considered before labeling a patient as having a primary respiratory disorder.

blogs.title: Choking Without Obstruction – The Neurogenic Dysphagia Alarm in Adults
blogs.description: Persistent choking that affects solids and liquids equally often leads clinicians down an ENT or gastroenterology pathway, yet a normal laryngoscopy and endoscopy should prompt a neurological workup. This article reviews the neurogenic dysphagia phenotype associated with brainstem pathology such as Chiari I malformation, differentiates it from myasthenia gravis, motor neuron disease and esophageal disorders, and proposes an algorithm that includes bedside swallow tests, videofluoroscopy patterns suggestive of central involvement, and early MRI of the craniocervical junction. Real‑world lessons from the case illustrate how earlier recognition could have prevented years of diagnostic delay.

blogs.title: The Hidden Chiari on a Routine Head CT – Radiologic Pearls for Frontline Clinicians
blogs.description: Chiary I is most often diagnosed by MRI, yet subtle clues may be present on plain head CT performed for unrelated reasons. This post presents a practical checklist for evaluating the posterior fossa on axial and sagittal reconstructions—looking for crowded foramen magnum, loss of CSF space, tonsillar protrusion toward the opisthion and bone crowding metrics. Using the case’s missed CT from fourteen years earlier as an illustration, it underscores the value of re‑reviewing old scans whenever new neurologic symptoms emerge and offers tips on communicating findings effectively to radiology colleagues.

blogs.title: Sleep Study Pitfalls in Brain‑Stem Respiratory Disorders – Why Type III May Miss the Real Problem
blogs.description: Portable type III sleep studies are convenient but lack EEG monitoring and often underestimate apnea‑hypopnea indices because they calculate events over total recording time rather than true sleep time. This article explains why patients with structural brainstem lesions may have modest AHI numbers despite profound desaturations dominated by central events. It compares type III versus full polysomnography with capnography in detecting central hypoventilation, outlines criteria for escalating to an attended study, and integrates practical guidance on interpreting mixed obstructive/central patterns when evaluating suspected Chiari‑related sleep apnea.

blogs.title: Scalp Pain in Chiari I – Decoding Vertex Allodynia, Nummular Headache & Burning Vertex Syndrome
blogs.description: Headache phenotypes associated with Chiari malformation are diverse and often mislabelled as primary headache disorders. This blog dissects the characteristics of occipital neuralgia, nummular headache and the newer burning vertex syndrome—all described in patients with tonsillar descent. It highlights clinical features such as cutaneous allodynia triggered by hair weight or light touch that responded dramatically to short haircuts in the presented case. The piece offers an assessment framework including pain maps, trigger point examination and targeted nerve blocks while calling attention to gaps in current symptom profiling tools.

blogs.title: "To Decompress or Not?" Decision‑Making for Posterior Fossa Decompression in Symptomatic Chiari I
blogs.description: When brainstem compression manifests as respiratory failure or neurogenic dysphagia, surgery becomes a pivotal option but carries its own risks. This post reviews contemporary evidence regarding outcomes after posterior fossa decompression—rates of symptom reversal for central hypoventilation, improvement in swallowing function and headache relief—against conservative strategies such as monitoring oximetry trends and lifestyle modifications. It outlines shared decision‑making principles tailored to patients hesitant about surgery like the one described, including counseling points on peri‑operative expectations, postoperative imaging surveillance schedules and criteria that trigger urgent operative referral.
